In the Land of the Gentle Monster, Take Off Your Sunglasses 
 KOREA SELATAN In the Land of the Gentle Monster, Take Off Your Sunglasses
 Despite the scorching sun, South Koreans prefer to wear hats and carry umbrellas. Sunglasses are rarely worn on a daily basis and are even considered somewhat impolite.
 07 Nov 2026 17:00 WIB · Internasional 
 AFP/ Jung Yeon-je
 Kecil Sedang Besar Sangat Besar Share
 Copy Link
 By Luki Aulia 
 This article has been translated using AI. See original . 
 00:00 00:00 10 10 1.00x Jennie Kim of K-pop group Blackpink and Karina of Aespa are both known for their sunglasses. They are both the faces of well-known eyewear brands Ray-Ban and Gentle Monster, respectively.
 However, the accessories that are a staple of K-pop stars' style are rarely seen on the streets of Seoul. South Koreans prefer to wear hats or umbrellas to protect themselves from the sun. Like soju and kimchi, Gentle Monster is apparently not selling well in its home country and is selling well abroad.
 This was reviewed in a report published in The Korea JoongAng Daily on Saturday (November 7, 2026). The newspaper, among other things, highlighted that in the Jongno area of ​​Seoul, pedestrians chose to carry umbrellas, wear hats, or cover their faces with masks to avoid sunburn.
 Some chose to seek shade or use their hands to shield their eyes, while only a few wore sunglasses. "People rarely wear sunglasses. Those who do might be seen as trying to stand out," said Im Ji-min, a student at Yonsei University.
 A rare habit of not wearing sunglasses was observed in a survey of 134 individuals in their 20s in South Korea. The poll was conducted in 2020 by a research team from Catholic Kwandong University.
 Research published in the Journal of the Korean Ophthalmic Optics Society (2026) showed that 76.1 percent of respondents rarely wore sunglasses. Despite their infrequent use, sunglasses are not unfamiliar.
 A survey by Real Optical Research involving 339 respondents revealed that 99 percent own at least one pair of sunglasses. However, this does not mean they are worn daily; most people tend to wear them only while on vacation, traveling abroad, or during weekends.
 In everyday life, sunglasses are considered more of a fashion accessory than a necessity for eye protection. The Korea Herald, June 30, 2026, reported that South Korean office workers prefer to wear umbrellas because they feel more comfortable and don't want to stand out from their colleagues. Sunglasses are even considered less appropriate for the office environment, similar to baseball caps.
 Social norms
 Ella Mitchell, an Australian employee living in South Korea, initially continued to wear sunglasses when leaving the office for lunch or meetings. However, as she often found herself to be the only person wearing them, she eventually switched to using an umbrella.
 Social norms influence the use of sunglasses. South Korean cultural psychologist Han Min explains that in societies shaped by Confucian traditions, such as South Korea and Japan, the eyes play a crucial role in conveying sincerity, attention, and respect. Therefore, covering the eyes with sunglasses during interactions can be perceived as diminishing an open impression.
 Sunglasses are often associated with a flashy style, particularly for some professionals. This accessory is more suitable for vacations, dates, or outdoor activities rather than for commuting to work or having lunch with colleagues.
 Emeritus professor of psychology at Seoul National University, Kwak Keum-joo, explained that the eyes play a crucial role in human communication. When the eyes are closed, eye contact becomes limited, and social distance feels greater. The conversation partner may perceive the individual as less sincere or less attentive to others.
 This perspective is rooted in history. Sunglasses gained popularity in South Korea during the Korean War (1950-1953), when many American soldiers wore them. The accessory then became associated with power and authority, particularly because former South Korean President Park Chung-hee frequently donned them alongside his military uniform.
 The association with power remains strong to this day. Kwak noted that the public perceives sunglasses differently when worn by celebrities or corporate leaders. For these prominent figures, the accessory is seen as a fashion statement. In contrast, ordinary people may feel awkward wearing them in their daily lives.
 Global industry
 On the other hand, the South Korean eyewear industry is rapidly expanding in the international market. Gentle Monster has emerged as a brand that boosts the popularity of South Korean eyewear through experimental designs, artistically conceived stores, and collaborations with celebrities and global fashion houses.
 The Korea Herald reports that Gentle Monster has 86 stores, 50 of which are outside South Korea. Its overseas revenue reached 332.9 billion won last year. The brand is expanding its collaborations with international brands such as Fendi, Moncler, and Maison Margiela.
 The South Korean eyewear market is projected to reach 4.7 trillion won by 2025, marking a 74 percent increase compared to 2022. The Seongsu area in Seoul has emerged as a key hub for the industry's growth, with eyewear stores in the region attracting a significant number of foreign buyers.
 Local residents, known as Warlok, have shown a preference for umbrellas. Sales of sun protection umbrellas at GS25 convenience stores surged by 351 percent in 2025 compared to 2024. From January to April 2026, sales increased further by 79.5 percent.
 This trend indicates that protection against ultraviolet (UV) rays is more commonly associated with skincare than with eye health. However, long-term UV exposure can increase the risk of cataracts and pterygium, which is the growth of tissue on the surface of the eye.
 The Korea Times, April 8, 2025, also stated that UV exposure can damage the retina and increase the risk of macular degeneration. Continuous exposure to UV rays in the eyes can accelerate tissue damage.
 Data from the National Health Insurance Service of South Korea indicates that cataract surgery was the most commonly performed surgical procedure in the country in 2023, with approximately 638,000 cases. The World Health Organization estimates that UV exposure is linked to one in five cataract cases worldwide.
 Ophthalmologist Shin Hyun-jin from Konkuk University Medical Center explained that the color of the iris can affect the dispersion of light within the eye. For instance, light blue irises can scatter more light compared to brown irises.
 Darker eye colors do not exempt individuals from the risk of UV damage. Protection is still necessary when engaging in outdoor activities, even on cloudy days, as UV rays remain present. Reflections from water and snow can also increase exposure.
 Eye doctors also caution that dark sunglasses without UV protection can actually increase the risk of eye damage. Dark lenses cause the pupils to dilate, allowing more light to enter the eyes.
 Therefore, individuals are advised to purchase sunglasses that can filter 99-100 percent of UV rays or carry a UV400 label. The lenses should also be wide enough to protect the eyes from sunlight entering from the sides.
